I played about with streaming services before they flopped (Gaikai, OnLive) and they worked okay, but the issue wasn't connection speed, but rather one of latency. There's no way I'd choose a noticeable delay in control (>.5s) over much tighter responsiveness on a local box. It's why steam's stream stuff works good, they limit it to the local network which means virtually no latency. When you're playing on a server that's 500 miles away and has 7 hops in between, it gets more and more difficult to compensate for the fact that what you press is not immediately registered in game. Now, latency isn't nearly as big an issue on OP's fiber as it is on, say, satellite internet, but the backbone and PoPs need to be hugely optimized before streaming will take off.
That's a really good point. There are some constraints beyond just throughput, and even if the experience is perfect there would have to be a compelling reason for gamers to give up local gaming.

For further examples, Valve's own TF2 uses a collection of tricks to deal with latency, summarized below

  1. Time travel. The server will rewind events slightly to correct for late commands from users.

  2. Forward prediction. The client predicts users movements based on their current direction and momentum. This is how you can get headshot around a corner without ever going around the corner. Their client "thought" you were going around the corner, and drew you being around the corner, without it ever actually happening.

  3. Drawing animations that never happened. When the prediction fails to correctly predict player movements, their player model has to speed up slightly or move in a way that it didn't actually move to navigate the world to "catch up" with its real position. Only really noticeable if you are multiplayer with another player and they can see what their own character is doing from both your screen and theirs.
